> I also have a 1941 Smith & Wesson .32 revolver and I don't know
> whether it is a .32 or a .32 S&W long.

The manufacturer's model number is on the top of the barrel, usually
between the front sight and the frame.  It will be something like
"V 3-5" or "M 3-5".  The number after the "V" or "M" tells you what
caliber it is.  A "3" is .32 S&W Long, a "5" is .38 Special.  A "V"
means "Victory", a "M" means "Military".

> I am thinking about getting a .32 Smith & Wesson, but I'm not
> sure whether to get a .32 or a .32 S&W Long.

Both are good guns.  The S&W Longs are hard to find, but if you can
find one, you can get the same amount of ammunition for half the
price.  The S&W Longs are also a little stronger and can be used for
carry guns.

The 32s are the best carry guns for women.  They are light, small, and
very easy to shoot.  A lady might not be able to handle a larger gun,
but she'll most likely do fine with the 32.  If she can't, you can
always get her a .22 revolver and teach her to shoot that.  The
revolvers are a lot easier to learn to shoot than the automatics.

It's called CapsLock, and it's designed to keep you (and your poor
keyboard) from accidentally typing in all caps.  It also makes it easier
to type in all caps, since it's only one key to press.

You can use Shift-CapsLock to toggle it on and off.  CapsLock is a
little tricky to use, since you have to press it twice in a row to
toggle it on (once to press it, once to let up on it), but once you
have CapsLock on, you can type whatever you want and it won't affect the
case of what you're typing.

I suspect this is due to a corrupted file, not a corrupted disk (although
you could have the same problem on either).  So, if you can't find the
file by any of the more obvious means, you may be able to recover it by
doing a file recovery.  This is a bit tricky, but I've done it several
times.  It works if the file is on the disk and has not been deleted
(although the file may not be in the same place where you remember it
being).  If you have an old version of Windows, try the following:

1)  Start the computer in DOS.
2)  Format the disk:
    a.  Insert the disk into the disk drive and then run FORMAT (or
        FORMAT A:, or whatever), but do not let it run all the way to
        completion.
    b.  When it asks you if you want to format the disk, type N and hit
        enter.
    c.  Then the format program will ask you if you want to create a
        directory on the disk.  Type N again and hit enter.
    d.  The FORMAT program will ask you if you want to format the disk
        again, and you should type Y and hit enter.  It will then
        format the disk again, but without making changes to the
        directory structure.  This will wipe out the bad sectors, but
        leave the directory structure alone.
3)  Run SCANdisk on the disk.  Again, I don't think you need to do a
    full scan, but you should run it at least once.  This will check the
    disk for errors and mark the bad sectors.
4)  Copy the files you want to recover from the disk to another disk.
    You can then abandon the disk that had the corrupted file and use
    the disk as a temporary disk to copy the files to a new one.
5)  If this doesn't work, you may have to reinstall Windows.  I don't
    know if you can recover the bad file this way, but it's worth a
    try.

>Is there a list of such companies out there?
>Or is it a matter of calling up every company and asking them?

There are a few places that have such listings, and you might want to
check them out.  One is the SIGGRAPH (Special Interest Group in
Computer Graphics) mailing list, which you can get by sending a message
with "subscribe SIGGRAPH" in the body of the message to "LISTSERV@SUNNY.UMD.EDU".

Another is the USENET newsgroup comp.graphics.misc


The mailings list is a bit more expensive, about $15-$25 a year, but it
is a lot more active.  The monthly mailing is mostly made up of
announcements of upcoming events, but it is always a good place to find
out about such things.

If you don't want to join the mailing list, you might try contacting
the SIGGRAPH mailing list person and ask them to send you a copy of the
"SIGGRAPH Yellow Pages" -- it is a listing of software companies and
individuals who are involved in computer graphics.  I don't know if
they will do this, but it is worth a try.

Try to avoid mailing lists.  They are usually a pain in the rear-end.
You are much better off posting to a newsgroup where you can talk to
people with the same problems that you have.  The people in a newsgroup
are much more friendly than the people in a mail list.  If you must try a
mail list, make sure that the list is moderated.  That way you can avoid
the jerks that try to get you to buy their products.

I've been working with X mostly on Sun's and SGI's.  I've had it on 2
IBM's, but it never worked well (especially their 3D acceleration) so I
took it off.  The XFree86 stuff seems to get better all the time, but I
don't have much experience with it.

To install X on my Sparcstations I use the install program on the
SunOS4.1.3 CDROM.  It will ask you what you want to install (this is a
menu driven program).  The only thing you need for X is the X11
package.  When you install that, make sure you install all of the X
packages.  I also install the window manager I want to use.  Usually I
use twm or fvwm.  I also install the xterm package.  If you install the
X11 package and the xterm package, then you will have X running pretty 
quickly.  If you install twm or fvwm, then your X will be fully
functional.

If you don't want to use the install program, then you will have to
compile and install X by hand.  Use the CDROM to get the sources and
follow the instructions in the INSTALL file in the X11 directory.  If you
don't like the way the SunOS4.1.3 X is compiled, then you can do a
"make clean" and then "make" and it will recompile everything.  This
takes a long time.

I have compiled and installed XFree86 on one of my Sun's, but I really
don't like it.  It supports my Trident card, but not my Diamond
Viper.  I think it's harder to configure.  I will probably go back to
SunOS4.1.3 X in a few weeks.

You need to know the model number of the card you want to use and also
the amount of memory it takes.  All of this is in the documentation for
the card.  This information is also in the Sun manual "SunOS System
Administration Guide: X Window System".  If you are going to use a
Trident card, then you will have to get the latest drivers from their
Web site.  The drivers on the Sun CDROM are not current.  They made a
change to the drivers in the last few months that makes them work
better.  I think the latest drivers are version 4.38.

You can also get the latest drivers from the XFree86 Web site.  I think
they have the latest drivers for the Trident cards.  I believe they have
drivers for the Diamond cards as well.

The term is "pixel", or "picture element".  Each of the dots (which are
actually squares) in a picture are pixels.  The highest rated monitors
are 1024x768x8 bit, or 1024x768 pixels with 8 bits per pixel.  This means
that the monitor can display 256 shades of gray, from black to white. 
1024x768 is the standard resolution of new video cards and monitors.  A
bit is the smallest unit of data.  In this case, it represents the
number of shades of gray in the picture.  The more bits, the more
shades of gray the monitor can display.  8 bit is the highest color
resolution available on most video cards and monitors.  The next one
up is 24 bit color, which supports 16.8 million colors.  This is
excellent for color images.  8 bit color is good for grayscale (black/
white) images, however.  The problem with 24 bit color is that it takes
up a lot of memory.  The standard video card memory is 1 MB, which
supports a 1024x768x8 bit image, or 768x1024x8 bit image.  A 24 bit
image takes up 4 MB, which is way too much for most video cards.  As a
result, most new video cards are limited to 8 bit color.  Some
companies are starting to sell 24 bit video cards, but they are very
expensive and have very little memory (256K).  They are also very slow,
because they have to "swap" colors, which means that they have to
change the colors of the screen when the colors change.  As a result,
they are best for viewing color images, but not for editing them.  A
popular monitor is the 17" SVGA monitor.  SVGA stands for Super VGA. 
The difference between SVGA and VGA is that it can support higher
resolutions.  The most common resolution is 1152x870.  The screen
resolution is determined by the number of pixels per inch.  Most
monitors are 12-14 pixels per inch, which means that 12-14 pixels are
displayed in one inch.  My monitor is 13 pixels per inch, which means
that it can support 1152x870x8 bit display (1152x870 pixels with 8 bits
per pixel).  For comparison, most Macintosh monitors are 14 pixels per
inch.  The difference is that the Mac monitor can only display 640x480x8
bit, which is a 13.3" screen.  The standard Mac monitor is 13" in size.

I am not an expert in this area, being a software engineer.  However, I
think the following is correct:

In order for a program to execute in a computer memory, the program must
be loaded into a specific (and usually fixed) location within the memory.
In a program that is loaded from disk, this means that the program must
be loaded from the disk to the correct memory location.  Note that a
program on disk is different from the program in memory.  A loaded
program in memory will not have the same contents as the program on disk;
the program in memory will have been changed by the operation of the
computer in response to the program and the program's data.  The program
on disk will be exactly the same regardless of whether it has been

I am not a member of the National Atheist Party.  I'm a member of the
American Atheists.

The National Atheist Party, which boasts an elected congressperson who
can be contacted through the American Atheists, is not a "party" in the
sense of a political party.  They have no "party platform" (except perhaps
to "defeat theism"), and their "platform" is purely a matter of
individual conscience.  They are not registered with the Federal
Government as a political party, and are not recognized as such.

The American Atheists, OTOH, is a registered membership organization
with a Board of Directors and a slate of officers.  It has a platform of
issues (not limited to atheism) which it promotes, and its officers are
"party officials".  For example, David Silverman, the current Chairman
of the American Atheists, is also the party Chairman.  The Executive
Director of the American Atheists is also the party's "Treasurer".

Thus, the American Atheists has officers, a platform, and a membership.
The National Atheist Party does not.

Reincarnation is the belief that the soul, the non-material part of
your being, is immortal, and that it is reborn in new bodies after
death.  The new body is usually a human body, but sometimes a nonhuman
body as well.  In other words, the essence of what you are is eternal,
and is never "killed" or annihilated.  The soul, or spirit, is the part
of you that is eternal.

The concept of reincarnation, or rebirth, is a very old one, and is
found in almost every religion of the world in one form or another.
Reincarnation is a belief that has existed in the East for many
thousands of years, and in the West it is a belief that has existed for
several thousand years.  It is a belief that has been held by many of
the great spiritual masters of the world, such as Buddha, Confucius,
Jesus, and Mohammed.  There is a great deal of evidence, both empirical
and testimonial, for the belief in reincarnation, but it is not a
belief that is taught by the world's organized religions.

Many people find the concept of reincarnation to be very comforting. It
gives them hope, for it teaches that death is not the end, that it is
possible to live forever.  On the other hand, many people find the
concept of reincarnation to be very disturbing, because it makes death
less of a certainty, and it makes it possible for them to lose control
of their eternal destiny.

I can't give you the name of a good place, but if you really want to
treat your car like a race car, it would be worth your effort to find
the right place.  Be sure to have them use high quality brake fluid
and frequent replacement of the fluid.  You should also have them
use a high quality brake pad material, if you plan to race.  They
should be able to advise you on the best material for your type of
racing.  If you need to, you can have them use disks that have been
machined to accept the grooved pads.

Racing uses a different brake lining than street use.  If you are
using racing pads, be sure to have them only used on the track.  The
discs will last much longer if you only use them for racing and
replace them after 5 or 6 track events.  The racing pads will wear
the disc very quickly if used on the street.  The pads will also wear
very quickly on the street.  I have had several sets of racing pads
wear out on the street in less than two years, whereas they will last
for 4 or 5 track events.

I usually use a light pedal pressure in the turns, and then keep the
pedal to the floor at an even level during the straightaway.  This
tends to keep the temperature of the brakes even and reduces the
chance of brake fade.  If you brake hard in the turns and let up in
the straights, you will generate a lot of heat, and when you take off
the brakes on the straights, you will get brake fade.  This will
beget more brake fade, and so on.  If you can keep the temperature
even, you will avoid the brake fade.  If you are running slicks on
the street, be sure to use a lot of pressure on the brakes, and
especially so in the corners.

The 486 chip is in a completely different ball park from the 386 chip. 
It is supposed to be 5-10 times faster.  The 486 chip is the same
architecture as the 386, it is a 32-bit chip.  The 386 is 16-bit.  The
386 chip is a little faster than the 286 chip, but this is only because
the 286 is a 16-bit chip.  The 286 chip was a compromise between a
16-bit and 32-bit chip.  It is not as fast as either.  The 386 chip is
not as fast as the 486 chip.  The 386 chip, as far as I know, does not
have a floating point chip (the FPU) on the chip.  The 486 chip has an
FPU on the chip.  The 486 chip is also a 32-bit chip.

This is a common problem.  The easiest way to fix it is to just run a
program that will disable the mouse and recover the mouse.  If you
don't have one handy, you can write one in C.  In the file /etc/mouse
is the interrupt mapping for the mouse.  This is what your program
should change.  It should not be too hard to write a program that reads
the file, then changes it to the correct one, and then executes a shell
command to restart the mouse.  You also have to cat the /etc/mouse file
into /etc/inittab so that it is read in at boot time.  Then you have
to run a shell command to disable the mouse.  Once the mouse is disabled
you can cat the /etc/mouse file to /etc/inittab and then restart the
mouse.

I just read a couple of articles in the Skeptical Inquirer attesting to
the efficacy of drinking water in the treatment of a number of physical
ailments.  It seems that this is quite old news to most of you, but I
found it very interesting and informative.

A study in India showed that Indians who drank more water were less
likely to contract intestinal illnesses than those who drank less.  At
first glance, this seems to be self-evident, but the Indian researchers
found that the benefits of water-drinking extended beyond the area of
the digestive tract.  Consumption of water was also correlated with a
decrease in the incidence of cancer, particularly of the bladder,
colon, and rectum.  They proposed that the protective effect of water is
related to its dilutional effects on carcinogens.

From that article, another study was cited which showed that in a
population of 4000 people in a Japanese community, there was a
significant increase in the incidence of disease in those who consumed
less than 1 liter of water per day as compared to those who consumed
more.  The diseases associated with water consumption were heart
attacks, high blood pressure, and strokes.  The researchers concluded
that "increasing fluid intake may decrease the risk of cardiovascular
disease."  The authors of this study also pointed out that the
protective effects of water is probably due to its dilutional effect on
toxins in the body, as well as its effect on regulating body temperature.

Another study cited in the Skeptical Inquirer showed that drinking water
may also help to reduce the incidence of kidney stones.  The researchers
found that people who consumed less than 1 liter of water per day were
more likely to contract kidney stones than those who drank more than 1
liter per day.

So if you're concerned about your physical health, try to get in the
habit of drinking a lot of water.  It's good for you!

What is the alternative to theism? Atheism? Agnosticism?
I think that agnosticism is not an alternative because it does not
provide any answers to the question of God. One could also say that
agnosticism is a position in which one is uncertain about the existence
of God, but I do not think that an agnostic has a position from which
he/she can argue against theism.

I think that atheism is the only real alternative to theism. If one
believes in some supernatural reality, then one is a theist, and
therefore believing in God. If one does not believe in such a reality,
then one is not a theist.

I think that one of the main problems with theists is that they believe
that the existence of God is self-evident. I do not think that it is
self-evident to a non-theist at all. And I do not think that one can
argue for God's existence and at the same time claim that God is
self-evident. This is just a contradiction. Either God's existence is
self-evident or it is not. If it is not, then one must argue for it.
If it is, then one has no reason to argue for it. If one cannot argue
for God's existence, then one must accept his/her own position of
atheism. I think that this is the only reasonable way to deal with the
question of God.

which means that the raw ERA (earned run average) is adjusted to an
equivalent ERA if the team played at the average run scoring level
throughout the season.

equal to the raw ERA.

The way you described it, I'd have to say it sounds like the bad sector
on the drive, but it may not be.  What you are doing is defragging the
drive, and I'm assuming that you are running the Mac through System 6.0.
The problem you might be having is that the sectors are all over the map,
and as you said, it takes a long time to sort them all out.  Try this:
run the Mac through System 7.0 or 7.1.  If you don't have the system
disk, you can get a copy at any Apple dealer or reseller.  The Mac will
find the bad sector and mark it as bad.  It will then defrag the drive
and mark each sector on the drive as good or bad.  Once it's done, you
can format the drive and it should work better.  Good luck.

Well, I don't have an answer for you, but I can share my experience with
the 500.  I replaced the battery in mine about a month ago, and it seems
fine.  I think that the battery can be replaced without taking the case
apart, but I opted to take it apart because I had a feeling that the
battery was the problem.  I found that the logic board was covered with
corrosion, and the corroded part was causing the battery to leak acid.
The acid had run down the board and come out of the logic board
connector, so the board was sketchy to say the least.

I cleaned everything up, replaced the battery, and soldered a new
connector to the logic board.

The 500 now seems to be working fine.  I would guess that the battery was
a bad one in the first place, which caused the acid to leak and corrode
the logic board.

Pseudo-Newtonian gravity field equations, in English:

In the Pseudo-Newtonian gravity field, gravity is caused by the 
bending of space by mass, not by the attraction of mass by mass. The 
gravity field is described in terms of potential energy by the equation: 

     1/2 m v^2 + 1/2 G m^2 / r - 1/2 G m sqrt(1 + 2 E / c^2) / r = const

where m is mass, v is velocity, G is the universal gravitational 
constant, r is distance from the center of mass, E is the total energy 
of the system (kinetic energy plus potential energy), and c is the speed 
of light. 

The first term is kinetic energy, the second term is the energy of 
attraction, and the third term is the energy of repulsion (the so-called 
"dark energy" of the universe). Noting that the energy of attraction is 
always negative, the energy of repulsion is always positive, and the 
magnitude of the energy of repulsion is twice the magnitude of the 
energy of attraction. 

The equations of motion are:

     m v = - dE / dr

and

     (d/dt) (m v) = F = - dE / dr - dE / dr - dE / dr

When E is less than zero, the equations of motion are the same as for 
Newtonian gravity, but with a reduced mass of m sqrt(1 + 2 E / c^2). 

When E is zero, the equations of motion are the same as for 
Pseudo-Newtonian gravity, which is compatible with Einstein's general 
theory of relativity. 

When E is greater than zero, the equations of motion for a body in 
free-fall toward a mass are:

     m v = - dE / dr = + G m sqrt(1 + 2 E / c^2) / r^2

     (d/dt) (m v) = F = + G m sqrt(1 + 2 E / c^2) / r^2 - + G m sqrt(1 + 2 E / c^2) / r^2

The second term is the force of repulsion, and the third term is the 
force of attraction. 

When E is greater than zero, the equations of motion for a body in 
free-fall away from a mass are:

     m v = - dE / dr = - G m sqrt(1 + 2 E / c^2) / r^2

     (d/dt) (m v) = F = - G m sqrt(1 + 2 E / c^2) / r^2 - - G m sqrt(1 + 2 E / c^2) / r^2

The second term is the force of attraction, and the third term is the 
force of repulsion. 

The equations of motion for circular motion of a body about a mass are:

     m v = - dE / dr = + G m sqrt(1 + 2 E / c^2) / r^2

     (d/dt) (m v) = F = + G m sqrt(1 + 2 E / c^2) / r^2 - + G m sqrt(1 + 2 E / c^2) / r^2

The second term is the force of repulsion, and the third term is the 
force of attraction. 

The energy of a body in circular motion is:

     1/2 m v^2 + 1/2 G m^2 / r - 1/2 G m sqrt(1 + 2 E / c^2) / r = 0

I have a very interesting encryption idea which I would like to discuss.
It is not a very advanced idea and I do not know if it will be useful, but
I think the idea is interesting.

I would like to know if some of you have heard about the ideas I am going
to explain, and what are you opinions about them. I would also like to
know if you have heard about them being tried.

Here is the basic idea:

Whenever I encrypt a message, I use a different key for each letter, but
the keys are the same for the same word in different messages. For example,
if the word "hello" appears in two messages, the same letter "h" will be
encrypted with the same key.

This idea has some advantages, because if someone intercepts two messages,
he cannot use the same plain text to try to find the key of each letter.

I would like to know if this idea has been tried, or if you know any
reference about it. If it has been tried, I would like to know about the
results.

Advantage of the 486DX/33 over the 486SX/33 is that the DX can handle
mathematical operations in the processor, while the SX has to pass the
information to the math co-processor, the 487SX.  That is why the DX/33
is about 25% faster than the SX/33, and the DX/50 is 45% faster than the
SX/33.  The advantage of the SX over the DX is that the SX has expandable
memory, while the DX has only 384KB of cache memory, and the DX/50 has
only 256K of cache memory.  If you put a 4MB SIMM in the SX, you can
have 4MB of memory, but only 256K of cache memory (unless you add a
cache card).  A 4MB SIMM in the DX/33 will give you 4MB of memory, but
only 384K of cache memory.

So the 486SX/33 is slower, but more expandable than the 486DX/33.  The
486DX/50 is faster, but not expandable.  The 486SX/50 is slower than
the 486DX/50, but it is expandable.

The "sunny-side up" answer is that you can, by using the
Lambert-Beer law and the atmospheric models.  In a nutshell, the
path length through the atmosphere is proportional to the total
atmosphere mass (M) and the secant of the zenith angle (theta).  The 
path length is also proportional to the extinction coefficient
(kappa) and proportional to the optical depth (tau) of the atmosphere.
The optical depth is the integral of the extinction coefficient 
with respect to the path length.  The opacity (beta) is the
ratio of the optical depth to the mass.

The total path length is then:

   Path = M * sec(theta) / (kappa * tau)

If you are interested in the amount of light reaching from an
object at altitude "h" , you can express the path length in
terms of "h" as:

   Path = 1 / (kappa * tau) * 1/(1 + h/Re)^(1/2)

where "R" is the radius of the earth and the factor in the parethesis 
is the secant of the zenith angle at altitude "h".  The optical
depth and opacity are functions of wavelength and altitude, and
are published in the NASA Spacecraft Planetary Data System (SPDS)
atmosphere files.  The SPDS files also have the optical depth
and opacity for the earth at various zenith angles, and are
also published in the "Encyclopedia of Planetary Sciences".

I recently needed to do just that.  I have a 486 DX2/66, and I needed
to boot from a floppy when I had no hard drive.  The client had a 486
SX/33, and I needed to boot from the hard drive, so I could modify the
disk.  I first tried to boot from a 3.3.1 diskette.  I could get past
the "initializing devices" screen, but as soon as it started to read
the hard drive, it went into a loop of "wait for drive 0 ..." and
" ... ok, go ahead" messages.  I think the only way to fix this is to
replace the hard drive controller with one that doesn't use DMA.

I then tried a 3.0 diskette.  The same problem occured.  I then
realized that the BIOS on the SX didn't know the hard drive was there
(duh).  I set the jumpers to slave, and then it was able to read the
hard drive.  I then tried floppies with 3.1, 3.3.1, and 4.0.  All
would work.  I then replaced the hard drive, set it to master, and
rebooted with the 4.0 diskette.  The system booted, and I was able to
get into DOS.  I then installed 4.0 from the network, and everything
worked fine.

your files back to your hard drive.

This is the "Daisy" theory of nuclear war. If you have not heard it
before, here it is. (It was first told to me by a well known artist
named Norman Rockwell. I think he made it up. I cannot vouch for the
authenticity of the story.)

There was once a little girl named Daisy. Daisy's father was a doctor.
One day, the father had to deliver a baby, and Daisy wanted to go
with him. He said, "Daisy, if I take you with me, you must promise
to be very quiet. If you make any noise, you will make the baby sick,
and the baby will die."

Daisy promised not to make a sound. The doctor and Daisy drove
to the house of the mother-to-be in his car. Daisy watched him
enter the house. Then she climbed up on the fender to watch the
street. The car was parked in front of a house.

A little while later, the baby was born. Daisy watched as the
doctor carried the baby out to the car. He placed the baby in the
front seat. Then he gently got into the driver's seat, and drove off
very slowly.

The doctor drove very slowly, but Daisy wanted to go faster. She
climbed into the back seat and stepped on the gas. The car leaped
forward, and Daisy fell off onto the street. The doctor stopped the
car, picked Daisy up, and carried her back to the house. 

The baby was very sick, and died the next day.

What Daisy learned from that experience is what is known as the
"Daisy Theory" of nuclear war.

I think that the problem you have is that you are assuming that "bits"
are similar to "bytes".  In fact they are completely different things.
"Bits" are the smallest possible pieces of information which computers
can handle.  A "bit" is either a 0 or a 1, and the computer cannot store
anything more than that.

A "byte" is a group of 8 "bits".  Thus, a byte can hold one of 256
different patterns of 0's and 1's, which is enough for the computer to
store a single letter of the alphabet.

people from buying a Pentium.  It was a great chip for it's time, but
isn't worth the extra money now.

If you are using an HP DeskJet 500 you probably have an HP Laserjet
printer driver installed.  This is a driver that allows the Macintosh to
talk to HP printers.  The driver is not specific to the DeskJet and will
not work with any other type of printer.

The DeskJet driver does not have a separate PostScript Interpreter
installed.  If you have the LaserJet driver installed on your machine you
have the PostScript Interpreter installed as well.  If you do not have the
LaserJet driver installed then you will have no PostScript support on your
machine even if you have an Adobe Type Manager installed.

The LaserJet driver can be installed through the printer driver
installations utility, it's easy to do, but you will need a LaserJet
printer.  You can also purchase the LaserJet driver from most Apple
stores.  It is also available from many computer stores, especially
specialized stores like the Computer Store in Santa Barbara.  I have
always been able to get the driver from them.

Good luck,

I'm sure the question is going to come up again,
so I think it is a good idea to make the following
observations.

    1.  As usual, the word "atheist" is a label, and
        a label that most people don't understand.
        It most often means that they are a non-
        religious person, or that they think religion
        is nonsense, or that they don't believe in
        a personal god.

        The word "atheist" literally means "without
        god", and it is this definition that is
        the most accurate.  It does not assert
        that there is no god, or that there is no
        place for god in the universe.  It simply
        means that there is no personal god.

    2.  The word "agnostic" is a label that is
        sometimes applied to those who claim that
        they don't know if there is a personal god
        or not.  It is a rather silly label, since
        it asserts that the person is not sure.
        In other words, they are expressing a lack
        of knowledge, and a lack of knowledge is
        not a valid argument to support a position.

    3.  The word "atheist" is not a valid label.
        If you say you are an atheist, you are
        actually saying that you don't know if
        there is a personal god or not.  As such,
        it is a silly label, and one that should
        be avoided.  It is not an accurate reflection
        of your position, and it is frequently
        misused and misunderstood.

    4.  The word "agnostic" is a valid label,
        but it is one that should be avoided as well.
        It is an acknowledgement of ignorance, and
        ignorance does not provide a valid basis
        for any argument.

    5.  If you want to be an atheist, fine.  If
        you want to be an agnostic, fine.  Just
        be careful about what you say, since much
        of it will be misunderstood, and some of
        it will be misused.

        The best thing to do is to just say what
        you mean.  If you want to say that you
        don't believe in a personal god, then say
        so.  If you want to say that you don't
        know if there is a personal god or not,
        then say so.  Just be careful about using
        labels, since they are frequently misunderstood
        and misused.

Answer:  The technology to do this is known as "multiplexed excitation"
and is a common technique for doing fluorescence microscopy.  The
advantages of this technology are that you have to do only one
excitation sweep to get the whole image, and you do not have to worry
about out-of-focus fluorescence.  Of course, you can't take a movie
with this system, but the speed advantage is enormous.  You can get
higher resolution with a scanning system, but you will find that you
can't really do the same kind of movie that the excitation-scanned
system can do.  One of the problems with scanning systems is that the
time for the scan is much longer than the time for the decay of the
fluorescence, so you will get very fuzzy pictures if you try to do a
movie.  There are some other problems with scanning systems, but
multiplexed excitation (ME) is the better way to do it.

ME systems have a number of drawbacks, however.  The main one is that
the excitation light is a bit intense (about 1/10 the maximum
intensity of the laser light), so you have to be careful to not look
at the sample out of focus or you will get a nasty burn on your retina.
The other drawback is that the system is not really intended to be a
"movie camera", although it can be used in this way.  The main
disadvantage of the ME systems is the cost.  A really good ME system
will cost about 10 times as much as a scanning system, and the
resolution of the images is not as good (about 1/3 the resolution of
the scanning systems).

fittings. I have a friend that is an auto mechanic and he made me a
cheap and simple carburetor cleaner. Its basically just a small
plastic storage box with a 3/8" copper tube going to a 3/8" copper

and rotor should be replaced with a new set.  If the distributor is
engaged properly, the engine should start and run fine.  There is a

touches the distributor housing.  The high tension wire screw should be
adjusted until it makes contact with the rotor.  The high tension wire
should be attached to the rotor.  Do not adjust the distributor cap or
rocker arms.  The distributor should be adjusted to the point where the
engine should start and run fine.  There is a rough adjustment that can

I think a lot of the junk about "statistically significant findings" is
due to the fact that a lot of people in the medical field don't have a
good understanding of statistics.  A lot of people in the medical field
think that a result is "statistically significant" if it is a result
that could not have occurred by chance alone.  If you have, say, 10
people in an experiment, and the result is that 8 of them got better
and 2 of them got worse, you would think that that is "statistically
significant" because it is unlikely that that would happen by chance
alone.  But if you look at it closely you can see that it is not
statistically significant.  The fact is that if you have only 10 people, 
the chances of that happening by chance are actually pretty good.  If
you have 1000 people, the chances of that happening by chance are very 
tiny.  So if you have a statistically significant result, you can make
the statement that the chances that this happened by chance are very
small, but you can't conclude that the result is due to your treatment
as opposed to chance.  It's like flipping a coin 10 times and getting 8
heads.  The chances of that are 1 in 1024 and it is unlikely that you
would get that by chance alone, but it is possible that you would get
that by chance alone.  

So when you hear the phrase "statistically significant result" you
should see if they also say that the chances of that happening by
chance are very small, and if they do try to find out how many people
they tested, because if it is only 10 people it isn't a very significant
result.

when you have a double slit experiment.  When you have a red filter in
front of one slit, and a blue filter in front of the other, and you
then view the resulting interference pattern, the color will be a
mixture of the red and blue.  (You should see a rainbow effect, if
you look at the colored fringes.)  What you will not see is
interference fringes for the colors in between red and blue.  I.e.
you will not see yellow fringes, or green fringes, etc.  (If you
have a really good eye, you may see a hint of yellow, but not a
distinct fringe.)  What you will see is interference fringes for the
reds and the blues, but no fringes for the greens, purples, etc.
This is what is called a "coherent" source.  (Incoherent sources
show no color mixing.)

My first response was "The Scam of the Century!"  But then I realized
what you were saying.  No, you're not in denial.  You're correct.  Your
SS# is not valid, but it's not for the reason you think.

SS#s are 9 digits long.  If your 9 digit number is preceded by a letter,
it's not a valid SS#.  To make it valid, you need to drop the letter and
add a 0 to the beginning.  Your SS# will then be 9 digits long.  Some
people have SS#s that are 8 digits long.  If your 8 digit number is
preceded by a letter, you need to drop the letter and add two 0's to the
beginning.  In this case, your SS# will be 10 digits long.

A good friend of mine is a former auto detailer, and he uses one of those flat
angle sponges to clean the car.  You can get these at the hardware store, and
they are used to clean floors.  They are maroon, and come in a plastic bag.

The above sponge is impregnated with a liquid soap (I think it's Dawn dish
soap), and it works quite well.  The nice thing about this sponge is that
it's washable.  It doesn't have a lot of dirt or grit in it, so it cleans
really well.  It won't leave any scratches or swirls in the paint.  For
really heavy dirt, you might want to use a soft sponge, or a good old
broom.  You can also use a really good car wash soap, which is available
in the auto section at most grocery stores.  They usually have a lot of
names, but the ingredients are pretty much the same.  You can also use
simple dish soap, but it's not quite as good.  You can also use a garden
hose to spray the car down.  Also, if you run your car over to the car
wash, try to get a foam wash, as the pressure washes can really scratch
the paint.

Another thing that can be done is to have your car waxed.  This will
help the dirt to slide off the paint.  Also if you have a clay bar, you
can use it to pull any fine grit or dirt off of the paint.  Then just
wash the car and wax it.  You can also use a good car polish to pull
off any minor scratches or swirl marks in the paint.  The trick here is
to use a polish with "wax" in the name.  This will fill in the scratches
and leave a nice wax on the paint.  I usually use "Meguiars" # 5 polish
on my car.  A soft cloth is used to apply the polish, and it can be
buffed out with a soft cloth.  I usually use a microfiber cloth.

I hope this helps.  Again, a car wax will do wonders for keeping dirt
off the paint.  A good wax will last for 3-4 months, and will give you
a nice shine to the car.  It also helps water to bead up and slide off
the paint, rather than to stay on the paint.  That's all I can think
of right now, but if you have any questions, feel free to ask.

Robert L. Riecks

On 27 Nov 1990 23:56:56 GMT,  [email protected]  (Tony) wrote:

> Is this a case of being stupid, or being a plant?

> If someone is stupid, then they might not understand the warnings
> about it being illegal, and they might continue as a result.

Well, the Feds are pretty much unwilling to bother with anyone who
isn't doing anything that's actually criminal.  And even then, unless
it's something big and/or newsworthy, they generally don't put much
effort into tracking down the guy who is selling the stuff, either.
A codebreaker who doesn't have any money to invest in a big, fancy
computer system (or doesn't know how to build one) is going to be
pretty limited in the kind of codes they could break, anyway.  I'd
guess that there's no way to crack a message encoded with a one-time
pad without having a copy of the pad, and that's a lot of bits to
store in your head, even if you're trained to memorize things.
Likewise, if you're just trying to figure out a particular code,
without having access to a treasure trove of messages encoded with
that code, you're pretty much out of luck.  You don't get any
information by encoding a message with a code you don't know.

Even if you did manage to encode a message with your own homemade
code, how would you actually send the message?  Without a radio,
a fax machine, or a cheap store-bought codebook, you'd have to
hand-write a letter, and mail it.  Assuming that the US Mail is
as slow as it used to be, it would take a couple of weeks for the
letter to get where it was going.  That wouldn't be much fun if
you're trying to send an urgent message, like a warning of an
imminent attack.

And then, once the letter arrived, it'd be pretty obvious what it
was, because most people don't write a lot of letters.  It'd stand
out like a sore thumb if you were writing half a dozen or more a
week.  If you're writing a lot of letters, you're probably doing
something else that's much more illegal than trying to write in
code.

The idea is that you have to add up the digits of the year to get the
Unix epoch date.  For example, 1990 is 1+9+9+0 = 19+9 = 28 = 2+8 = 10,
which is 80+10 = 90.  The year 1991 would be 1+9+9+1 = 19+9+1 = 29 = 2+9 =
11, which is 1+1 = 2.  1992 would be 1+9+9+2 = 20+9+2 = 30+2 = 32 = 3+2 = 5.
The year 2000 would be 2+0+0+0 = 20+0+0 = 20, which is 2+0 = 2.  So in
Unix time, the year 2000 is identical to the year 1992.

The year 1996 would be 1+9+9+6 = 19+9+6 = 29+6 = 35 = 3+5 = 8.

The year 1997 would be 1+9+9+7 = 19+9+7 = 29+7 = 36 = 3+6 = 9.

It's an old trick, but the idea's still there.

The Left-handed hitter is an interesting phenomon.  From my experience as
a player and coach, I have found that the left-handed batter is more
difficult to pitch to than the right-handed batter.  This is because the
left-handed hitter is more difficult to position in the zone.  A
right-handed pitcher will hold the ball on the outside of the plate after
the hitter is ready to swing.  If the hitter is right-handed, the ball
will be on the inside of the plate.  The left-handed hitter will have
more difficulty because the ball is on the outside of the plate and the
hitter will tend to swing early.  If the ball is inside, the hitter will
swing late.  Also, the ball will tend to break on the right-handed hitter
away from the hitter and into the strike zone while it will tend to break
on the left-handed hitter towards the hitter.  This is because a right-
handed pitcher will tend to throw a pitch towards the right-handed
hitter's hands and away from the left-handed hitter's hands.  This makes
the left-handed hitter more difficult to pitch to.  Also, the left-
handed hitter will tend to have better control of his swing because he
will tend to swing towards the pitcher and not away from the pitcher.

This is a good question, and a good point.  I have a Macintosh
Quadra 900 somewhere that I need to get around to installing
an image on.  I'm not quite sure how to do it, but here's what
I would suspect the process to be in general:

1) Make sure you have the proper software to do it.  Make sure you
   have a boot disk for the machine, and the appropriate
   software to create an image.  If you don't have the software,
   you may have to buy it.

2) Determine what size image you want.  This will depend on
   the size of the partition on your hard drive, and how much
   room you want to leave for other stuff.  You can use the
   following equation to determine how much space you will need:

      (size of image) * 3 = (size of image + overhead) = (size
      of hard drive partition - space for other stuff)

3) Prepare the hard drive partition.  This may be something as
   simple as running fdisk on your boot disk, or it may be
   something more complicated.

4) Copy the image onto the hard drive.

5) Configure the image to boot.  This is a more complex
   process.  Boot the image with the boot disk, and run the
   image setup software, assuming you have it.

6) Perform any other configuration you need to do for the
   image, such as configuing the network, or other hardware
   and software.

7) Install the image.  This may be something as simple as
   running the install program, or it may be a more complex
   process.

8) Install any software you need to install.

9) Install any hardware drivers you need to install.

10) Configure the image to your liking.

11) Boot the image from the boot disk.  This will probably be
    necessary the first time you boot it, and maybe the second
    time, too.  If you have properly configured the image, it
    will boot into it.

12) Enjoy.

I realize that this is not exactly what you're looking for, but it is very
easily to change your 3.1 machine to run NT.  This works both ways also
(same hardware, different OS's).  The current version of NT will run fine
on a 486/66 machine with 16 megs of RAM and a 170MB hard drive (that's
what I'm running).  It also runs very well on a 486/50 with 8 megs of RAM
and a 200 MB hard drive.  The NT setup program will allow you to create a
small drive partition (around 100 megs I think) which you can use to
install WinNT.  You can then use your main drive to store your data, and
use the small partition to run WinNT.

The setup program for NT is very nice.  It will allow you to create
multiple partitions, and to create a boot disk for either WinNT or DOS.
You can then choose which OS you want to boot at startup.  It will also
allow you to upgrade your hard drive while installing (it will actually
install to the new drive and then copy all your data from the old drive to
the new).

I recommend the 3.1 install to a small partition for two reasons:  First,
it will save you an upgrade to 3.11.  Secondly, it will allow you to
upgrade to NT without having to repartition your drive.  I have had
nothing but success with this setup.  I just had NT installed on my old
486/50, and it runs like a champ.  The main thing is to get the RAM up
to at least 16 megs, or the machine won't run very well.  I kept my 3.1
drive as a backup (I have an external drive bay for it), but I have not
bothered to install it again (I thought I might need it for something, but
have yet to find an application that works better under 3.1 than under
NT).

I hope this helps.  It works much better than I expected.  I have been
using my old 486 as the main machine in the house for about a month now.
We have a 486/66 with Win3.1 as the secondary machine.

Good luck,

Anyway, in the old days, the way to get a quick and dirty Xterm font
was to take the font you wanted and run it through the makefont
program that came with the X11 distribution.

  makefont -b -a -n <fontname> <fontfile>

Then, you would copy the file that makefont generated into the fonts
directory, and the font would show up when X was restarted.

The problem with this, of course, is that you would have to restart
X every time you wanted to use a different font.  Today, most of
us are running X11 in the background as a window manager, so
you'd have to restart X everytime you wanted to change fonts.

There are two ways to do this.  One method is to create an entry
in your X resource file that looks like this (or something similar):

  XTerm*font: <fontname>

That way, whenever you started an Xterm, it would use the font you
specified.  However, if you were running an Xterm already, you'd
have to type in "xrdb" to read the resource file before the font
change would take effect.  You could also use the "xrdb -merge"
command to merge the new resource file into the existing resource
database.

The second method is to write a shell script that creates a new
X resource file, merges it into the existing resource file, and
then starts a new Xterm.  This way, you get a different font every
time you start a new Xterm, without having to restart X.  I don't
have time to write one for you, but you could easily do it yourself
with the "cat", "echo", and "xrdb" commands.

I have never tried this myself, but I understand that the
Xresource program lets you do something similar from within the
Xterm window itself.  I believe that this functionality is part of
the new X11R5 release, but I could be wrong.
